name: Example: Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Substitution
problem:
Find the general solution to the following first-order ODE using the substitution $z=y^3.$

$$
xy^2\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} = x^2+y^3
$$
worked_solution:
Let's make a substitution

$$
z=y^3\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}=3y^2\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y^2\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{3}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

 Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{3}\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}\right)=x^2+z
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3}{x}({x}^{2}+z) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =3x+\frac{3}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{3}{x}\,z & =3x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-\frac{3}{x},\,Q(x)=3x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-3/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{3}{x}\,z) & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\cdot 3x \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{3}{{x}^{4}}\,z & =\frac{3}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{z}{{x}^{3}}) & =\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{z}{{x}^{3}})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\text{d}x \\ \frac{z}{{x}^{3}} & =-\frac{3}{x}+C \\ z & =-3{x}^{2}+C{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z=y^3.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3} & =z \\ {y}^{3} & =-3{x}^{2}+C{x}^{3} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{-3{x}^{2}+C{x}^{3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$
